Babylon-Iraq.name: Babylon
Babylon-Iraq.evidence_basis: Rose from a ~25 ha Akkadian town to ~280 ha under Hammurabi, suffered Sennacherib's 689 BC destruction, and expanded under Nebuchadnezzar II to ~900 ha within outer walls (~185 inh/ha across built quarters; George 1992; Baker 2022).

Nineveh-Iraq.name: Nineveh
Nineveh-Iraq.evidence_basis: 40-45 ha in Late Chalcolithic (Stronach 1994), expanding to a 750 ha walled imperial metropolis under Sennacherib (~150 inh/ha across residential zones and royal parks; Ur 2005, 2013b), catastrophically depopulated after the 612 BC sack.

Nimrud-Iraq.name: Nimrud
Nimrud-Iraq.evidence_basis: Founded by Shalmaneser I and enlarged by Ashurnasirpal II (879 BC) to 360 ha (20 ha citadel + 340 ha lower town; Oates and Oates 2001; Ur 2013b; ~175 inh/ha), declining after capital transfer to Nineveh and collapsing after 612 BC.

Uruk-Iraq.name: Uruk
Uruk-Iraq.evidence_basis: Expanded from 250 ha in Late Uruk (Finkbeiner 1991) to a 400 ha walled metropolis in Early Dynastic I-III (~125 inh/ha; Adams and Nissen 1972; Adams 1981), contracting in the second millennium before a Neo-Babylonian revival (~190 ha).

Lagash-Iraq.name: Lagash
Lagash-Iraq.evidence_basis: Multi-centric marsh-edge city spanning 400-500 ha including canals, gardens, and lagoons (~280-320 ha dense residential at ~140 inh/ha in ED III; Carter; Hammer 2022), declining sharply after administrative shift to Girsu and OB river changes.

Ur-Iraq.name: Ur
Ur-Iraq.evidence_basis: 60 ha walled core plus extensive extramural suburbs totaling ~100-120 ha as Ur III imperial capital (Woolley and Mallowan 1976; Wright 1981; Hammer 2019), sacked by Elam in 2004 BC, recovering in Old Babylonian and Neo-Babylonian rebuilds.

Dur-Sharrukin-Iraq.name: Dur-Sharrukin
Dur-Sharrukin-Iraq.evidence_basis: 288-300 ha planned square imperial capital built by Sargon II (Parpola 1995; Loud 1936; partially settled at ~120 inh/ha upon 706 BC inauguration), abruptly abandoned as royal seat after Sargon's death in 705 BC.

Umma-Iraq.name: Umma
Umma-Iraq.evidence_basis: Expanded to ~250-300 ha in Early Dynastic III and served as a major Ur III provincial capital (Adams 1981; Steinkeller 2007; Rost 2015), contracting heavily after the Old Babylonian collapse of central Sumerian canals.

Larsa-Iraq.name: Larsa
Larsa-Iraq.evidence_basis: Walled oval city of ~190-200 ha at its peak under Rim-Sin I (Huot 1989; Adams 1981; ~175 inh/ha), declining after Hammurabi's conquest in 1763 BC and Samsu-iluna's southern crisis, with Kassite and Neo-Babylonian Ebabbar revivals.

Kish-Iraq.name: Kish
Kish-Iraq.evidence_basis: Extensive twin-city complex (Kish and Hursagkalama) spanning ~180-200 ha across multiple mounds in ED I-III (~165 inh/ha; Gibson 1972; Moorey 1978), remaining a major Babylonian urban center through Neo-Babylonian rebuilds.

Girsu-Iraq.name: Girsu
Girsu-Iraq.evidence_basis: Religious and political capital of Lagash state under Gudea and Ur III governors, reaching ~200-250 ha multi-mound extent (~135 inh/ha across occupied quarters; Parrot 1948; Rey 2016), declining to a modest town from Old Babylonian onward.

Nippur-Iraq.name: Nippur
Nippur-Iraq.evidence_basis: Pan-Sumerian sacred seat of Enlil covering 135-150 ha within walls in ED III-Old Babylonian periods (~180 inh/ha; Adams 1981; Gibson 1992; Stone 1987), briefly depopulated c. 1720 BC before Kassite and Neo-Babylonian restorations.

Dur-Kurigalzu-Iraq.name: Dur-Kurigalzu
Dur-Kurigalzu-Iraq.evidence_basis: Kassite royal capital founded by Kurigalzu I enclosing ~225-300 ha of palaces, ziggurat, and dispersed residential quarters (~110 inh/ha effective density; Baqir 1944; Clayden 1996), declining rapidly after Elamite sacks c. 1155 BC.

Adab-Iraq.name: Adab
Adab-Iraq.evidence_basis: Multi-mound complex spanning ~180-200 ha effective residential area within a broader ~300-400 ha Early Dynastic-Akkadian urban zone (Banks 1912; Adams 1981; Marchetti et al. 2019), declining after Ur III.

Arbela-Iraq.name: Arbela
Arbela-Iraq.evidence_basis: 10 ha citadel attested from 2300 BC expanding into a major ~150-200 ha lower town as the Ishtar sanctuary and eastern pillar of the Assyrian imperial core (Novacek 2011; Ur et al. 2013; ~150 inh/ha), surviving 612 BC.

Borsippa-Iraq.name: Borsippa
Borsippa-Iraq.evidence_basis: Twin sacred city to Babylon housing the Ezida temple of Nabu, expanding to ~140-160 ha within Neo-Babylonian walls (~165 inh/ha; Allinger-Csollich 1998; Baker 2022).

Isin-Iraq.name: Isin
Isin-Iraq.evidence_basis: Reached ~150 ha as capital of the First Dynasty of Isin (~160 inh/ha; Hrouda 1977; Adams 1981), later experiencing a major resurgence as political center of the Second Dynasty of Isin under Nebuchadnezzar I.

Mari-Syria.name: Mari
Mari-Syria.evidence_basis: Planned circular 110 ha walled hydraulic metropolis (~60 ha densely occupied inner city at peak; Margueron 2004; ~350+ inh/ha core / ~215 overall), thriving under ED III and Zimri-Lim before Hammurabi's 1761 BC destruction.

Sippar-Iraq.name: Sippar
Sippar-Iraq.evidence_basis: Walled northern Babylonian Shamash cult center covering ~100-120 ha (~180 inh/ha; Gasche and De Meyer; Jursa 1995), famed for its naditu cloister in OB times and Ebabbar temple library in the Neo-Babylonian era.

Shuruppak-Iraq.name: Shuruppak
Shuruppak-Iraq.evidence_basis: Peaked at ~100-120 ha in Early Dynastic IIIa when Fara administrative tablets document dense urban wards and granaries (~170 inh/ha; Martin 1988; Otto et al. 2018), contracting to ~55 ha in Ur III before Old Babylonian abandonment.

Bad-tibira-Iraq.name: Bad-tibira
Bad-tibira-Iraq.evidence_basis: Sumerian metallurgical and Dumuzi cult center reaching ~115-130 ha at its Early Dynastic III maximum (~145 inh/ha; Adams 1981; Crawford 1960), fortified under Sin-iddinam of Larsa before declining in the mid-second millennium.

Cutha-Iraq.name: Cutha
Cutha-Iraq.evidence_basis: Major northern Babylonian cult center of Nergal covering ~85-110 ha across its central and outer tells (~160 inh/ha; Adams 1972; Gibson 1972), prominently expanded in the Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian eras.

Tell Mozan-Syria.name: Tell Mozan
Tell Mozan-Syria.evidence_basis: Expanded from ~15 ha to a 120-135 ha walled Hurrian royal capital in EJ III-IV (Buccellati and Kelly-Buccellati 2002; Pfalzner et al. 2004; ~135 inh/ha), persisting through the 4.2 ka BP crisis before contracting in MBA-Mitanni times.

Tell Taya-Iraq.name: Tell Taya
Tell Taya-Iraq.evidence_basis: 155 ha late third-millennium walled stone-founded city whose entire street and house layout was surface-mapped (~110 inh/ha including open courtyards; Reade 1973, 1997; Pfalzner 2001), contracting sharply in MBA-Iron Age.

Dur-Katlimmu-Syria.name: Dur-Katlimmu
Dur-Katlimmu-Syria.evidence_basis: Expanded from a ~15 ha MBA town to a 55-60 ha Middle Assyrian seat and 110 ha walled Neo-Assyrian regional metropolis on the Lower Khabur (Kuhne 1995, 2011; ~155 inh/ha), remaining active under Neo-Babylonian governance.

Mashkan-Shapir-Iraq.name: Mashkan-Shapir
Mashkan-Shapir-Iraq.evidence_basis: 72 ha walled secondary capital of Larsa dissected by canals with mapped residential, craft, and temple districts (Stone and Zimansky 2004; ~220 inh/ha on built areas = ~15k-17k), abandoned c. 1720 BC after Tigris channel shift and revolt.

Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta-Iraq.name: Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta
Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta-Iraq.evidence_basis: Middle Assyrian royal foundation across the Tigris from Assur enclosing ~240 ha total with a ~64 ha walled palace/temple core (Dittmann 1990; ~15k-16k brief peak before Tukulti-Ninurta I's 1197 BC assassination).

Tell Brak-Syria.name: Tell Brak
Tell Brak-Syria.evidence_basis: 130 ha LC3 indigenous urban peak (55 ha dense core + variable-density outer town; Ur et al. 2007, 2011; McMahon 2020), contracting in LC4-EJ II, re-expanding to 65-70 ha as Akkadian Nagar (~165 inh/ha; Oates et al. 2001) and Mitanni palace center.

Assur-Iraq.name: Assur
Assur-Iraq.evidence_basis: 56-65 ha cliff-top religious and commercial capital of Assyria with densely packed merchant quarters (Andrae 1938; Miglus 1996; ~220-240 inh/ha), sacked by Cyaxares' Medes in 614 BC.

Eshnunna-Iraq.name: Eshnunna
Eshnunna-Iraq.evidence_basis: Diyala kingdom capital spanning ~40-50 ha densely built residential blocks and royal palaces (~290 inh/ha at OB peak per Delougaz et al. 1967; Adams 1965), declining sharply after Hammurabi's 1762 BC conquest.

Tell Hamoukar-Syria.name: Tell Hamoukar
Tell Hamoukar-Syria.evidence_basis: Restricted to 15 ha main mound in LC3-4 after LC1-2 Khirbat al-Fakhar's abandonment, then expanded to a 98-105 ha walled EBA city (Ur 2002b, 2010b; Gibson et al. 2002; ~140 inh/ha) before collapsing post-2200 BC.

Arrapha-Iraq.name: Arrapha
Arrapha-Iraq.evidence_basis: Capital of the Hurrian kingdom of Arraphe and later a core Neo-Assyrian provincial capital (~65-80 ha citadel and lower town beneath Kirkuk; Stein; Radner 2006; ~175 inh/ha).

Zabalam-Iraq.name: Zabalam
Zabalam-Iraq.evidence_basis: Important Inanna cult city in the Umma province spanning ~75-85 ha in Early Dynastic I-III (~160 inh/ha; Adams 1981; Powell 1976), maintaining regional status under Ur III and Larsa before Old Babylonian contraction.

Tell Leilan-Syria.name: Tell Leilan
Tell Leilan-Syria.evidence_basis: Grew from ~15 ha to a 90 ha planned walled city in EJ III-IV (~150 inh/ha; Weiss et al. 1993; Ristvet 2007), depopulated in the 2200 BC Habur Hiatus, revived as Shamshi-Adad I's 90 ha capital Shubat-Enlil, and destroyed by Samsu-iluna in 1728 BC.

Marad-Iraq.name: Marad
Marad-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~75-85 ha walled city of Lugal-Marada on the Arahtu Euphrates branch (Adams 1981; Al-Hussainy 2010; ~155 inh/ha), thriving under Akkadian, Old Babylonian, and Neo-Babylonian patronage.

Opis-Iraq.name: Opis
Opis-Iraq.evidence_basis: Strategic Tigris-Diyala river emporium (~60-75 ha surveyed mound complex; Adams 1965; ~175 inh/ha), serving as the eastern anchor of Nebuchadnezzar II's Median Wall and site of the 539 BC Battle of Opis.

Kurd Qaburstan-Iraq.name: Kurd Qaburstan
Kurd Qaburstan-Iraq.evidence_basis: 105 ha walled MBA capital identified with Qabra on the Erbil Plain (42 ha dense inner core + partly hollow walled lower town; Ur et al. 2013; Schwartz et al. 2017; ~115 inh/ha overall), declining steadily from LBA onward.

Nigin-Iraq.name: Nigin
Nigin-Iraq.evidence_basis: Third urban center of the Lagash state and sacred city of Nanshe, covering ~70 ha across two main mounds in ED III-Ur III (~155 inh/ha; Nadali and Polcaro 2016), contracting in Old Babylonian times.

Tell Halaf-Syria.name: Tell Halaf
Tell Halaf-Syria.evidence_basis: 55-60 ha walled Aramean Bit-Bahiani capital and Neo-Assyrian provincial seat on the Khabur headwaters (von Oppenheim 1943; Novak 2013; ~185 inh/ha), declining after Assyria's collapse.

Tell Khoshi-Iraq.name: Tell Khoshi
Tell Khoshi-Iraq.evidence_basis: 92 ha fortified Early Bronze Age city south of Jebel Sinjar (~115 inh/ha across walled lower town; Lloyd 1938; Kepinski-Lecomte 2001), suffering severe depopulation during the post-2200 BC aridification.

Tell al-Wilaya-Iraq.name: Tell al-Wilaya
Tell al-Wilaya-Iraq.evidence_basis: Fortified Tigris-corridor urban mound of ~60-70 ha with monumental Early Dynastic and Akkadian administrative buildings (Madhloum 1960; Hussein et al. 2009; ~155 inh/ha), shrinking after Ur III.

Til Barsip-Syria.name: Til Barsip
Til Barsip-Syria.evidence_basis: 50-60 ha Euphrates crossing city thriving as Luwian/Aramean Masuwari and then Shalmaneser III's western imperial stronghold Kar-Shalmaneser (Thureau-Dangin 1936; Bunnens 1997; ~180 inh/ha).

Tell Chuera-Syria.name: Tell Chuera
Tell Chuera-Syria.evidence_basis: 65-80 ha circular walled Kranzhugel EBA city with planned radial streets and Palace F (Orthmann 1995; Meyer 2007; ~140 inh/ha), abandoned c. 2200 BC and partially reoccupied as Middle Assyrian Harbe.

Abu Salabikh-Iraq.name: Abu Salabikh
Abu Salabikh-Iraq.evidence_basis: 10 ha Uruk mound (Pollock 1990) expanding to 50 ha total (~25-30 ha densely packed Main and West mounds) in ED III (~300+ inh/ha in walled residential core per Postgate 1994), abandoned during the Akkadian period.

Der-Iraq.name: Der
Der-Iraq.evidence_basis: Strategic eastern frontier fortress-city of ~55-65 ha near modern Badra controlling the Zagros road to Susa (~150 inh/ha; Oates 1966; De Meyer), site of the 720 BC battle between Assyria and Elam.

Tell Baqrta-Iraq.name: Tell Baqrta
Tell Baqrta-Iraq.evidence_basis: 4 ha Chalcolithic high mound that expanded across an 80 ha lower town in late EBA (~120 inh/ha; Ur et al. 2013; Kopanias et al. 2016), contracting sharply in MBA, reviving to 20 ha in LBA, and shrinking to a 5 ha Neo-Assyrian village.

Emar-Syria.name: Emar
Emar-Syria.evidence_basis: 50-60 ha Euphrates entrepot refounded on an elevated terrace by Hittite kings in the 14th century BC with rich cuneiform archives (Margueron 1982; Fleming 2000; ~165 inh/ha), destroyed c. 1187 BC.

Tell ed-Der-Iraq.name: Tell ed-Der
Tell ed-Der-Iraq.evidence_basis: 55 ha walled sister city of Sippar dedicated to Annunitum, extensively excavated by the Belgian expedition (De Meyer 1978; Gasche 1989; ~165 inh/ha at Old Babylonian peak).

Bakr Awa-Iraq.name: Bakr Awa
Bakr Awa-Iraq.evidence_basis: 50-60 ha Shahrizor Plain urban center with fortified lower town and citadel (Miglus et al. 2013; Altaweel et al. 2012; ~155 inh/ha), serving as the Neo-Assyrian eastern stronghold of Dur-Assur.

Qasr Shemamok-Iraq.name: Qasr Shemamok
Qasr Shemamok-Iraq.evidence_basis: 50 ha walled Middle and Neo-Assyrian provincial capital of Kilizu with up to 30 ha of extramural LBA industrial and residential sprawl (Rouault and Masetti-Rouault; Ur et al. 2013; ~150 inh/ha).

Tell al-Hawa-Iraq.name: Tell al-Hawa
Tell al-Hawa-Iraq.evidence_basis: 50 ha LC2-3 center (18 ha core + 32 ha diffused outer town), contracting in LC4-5 and expanding to a 66 ha three-tier urban apex in EJ III-IV (Ball et al. 1989; Wilkinson and Tucker 1995; ~140 inh/ha), continuing as a Middle/Neo-Assyrian town.

Imgur-Enlil-Iraq.name: Imgur-Enlil
Imgur-Enlil-Iraq.evidence_basis: 64 ha square walled Neo-Assyrian royal palace-fortress town built by Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III east of Nimrud (Oates 1974; Curtis and Tallis 2008; ~135 inh/ha), sacked in 614-612 BC.

Tulul al-Baqarat-Iraq.name: Tulul al-Baqarat
Tulul al-Baqarat-Iraq.evidence_basis: Multi-mound archaeological complex identified with ancient Kesh (~45-55 ha occupied urban core across mounds TB1-TB7; Lippolis 2016, 2020; ~155 inh/ha), showing ED-Isin-Larsa peak and Neo-Babylonian temple revival.

Tuttul-Syria.name: Tuttul
Tuttul-Syria.evidence_basis: 40-45 ha urban center at the Balikh-Euphrates confluence housing the famous Dagan sanctuary and palaces (Strommenger and Kohlmeyer 2000; Miglus 2007; ~175 inh/ha at EBA-MBA peak), declining in the Late Bronze Age.

Tutub-Iraq.name: Tutub
Tutub-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~30-35 ha Diyala city excavated around the Temple Oval and dense Early Dynastic walled residential quarters (Delougaz 1940; Adams 1965; ~220 inh/ha), declining after the Old Babylonian period.

Me-Turan-Iraq.name: Me-Turan
Me-Turan-Iraq.evidence_basis: Hamrin Basin walled city enclosing ~72 ha with a dense ~35-45 ha inner core and extensive literary/temple archives (Al-Rawi and Black 1989; Cavigneaux 1999; ~165 inh/ha at OB and Neo-Assyrian peaks).

Tell Hadidi-Syria.name: Tell Hadidi
Tell Hadidi-Syria.evidence_basis: 55 ha walled Early Bronze Age regional city on the Syrian Euphrates (~140 inh/ha; Dornemann 1979; Cooper 2006), contracting to the ~15 ha high mound as Late Bronze Age Azu.

Dilbat-Iraq.name: Dilbat
Dilbat-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~35-45 ha agricultural and Urash temple town south of Babylon well attested in Old Babylonian economic archives (Armstrong 1992; ~165 inh/ha), remaining active through the Neo-Babylonian period.

Ekallatum-Iraq.name: Ekallatum
Ekallatum-Iraq.evidence_basis: Royal seat of Shamshi-Adad I and Ishme-Dagan I north of Assur (~40-45 ha estimated from Mari/Assyrian royal archives and Tigris survey mounds; Charpin and Ziegler 2003; ~175 inh/ha).

Terqa-Syria.name: Terqa
Terqa-Syria.evidence_basis: Heavily fortified Euphrates city (~30-40 ha including eroded riverbank sector; Buccellati 1988; Rouault 2004; ~190 inh/ha), rising as capital of the Kingdom of Hana after Mari's fall and continuing as Neo-Assyrian Sirqu.

Kisurra-Iraq.name: Kisurra
Kisurra-Iraq.evidence_basis: 45 ha town north of Shuruppak that flourished as an independent Isin-Larsa city-state (Kienast 1978; Adams 1981; ~165 inh/ha), declining after absorption into Babylon's provincial network.

Anat-Iraq.name: Anat
Anat-Iraq.evidence_basis: Fortified Euphrates island and riverbank capital of the Suhu polity (~35-45 ha combined island and terrace settlement attested in Mari archives and Suhu royal inscriptions; Northedge et al. 1988; ~165 inh/ha).

Abu Tbeirah-Iraq.name: Abu Tbeirah
Abu Tbeirah-Iraq.evidence_basis: 42-45 ha harbor town east of Ur equipped with an excavated artificial basin connected to the Gulf marshes (Romano and D'Agostino 2018; Forti et al. 2022; ~150 inh/ha), declining after early second-millennium siltation.

Rapiqu-Iraq.name: Rapiqu
Rapiqu-Iraq.evidence_basis: Strategic Middle Euphrates gateway town near modern Fallujah (~35-45 ha estimated from Old Babylonian Mari/Hammurabi correspondence and Middle/Neo-Assyrian campaign itineraries; Charpin 2004; ~150 inh/ha).

Samarra-Iraq.name: Samarra
Samarra-Iraq.evidence_basis: Ancient Tigris crossing and Neo-Assyrian fortified town of Sur-Marrati (~35-45 ha settled zone beneath later horizons, attested in Sennacherib's royal annals; Northedge 2005; ~150 inh/ha).

Tarbisu-Iraq.name: Tarbisu
Tarbisu-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~40 ha walled Neo-Assyrian satellite city north of Nineveh housing the crown prince's palace and Nergal temple (Suleiman 1971; Reade 1978; ~165 inh/ha), destroyed by Medes in 614 BC.

Hit-Iraq.name: Hit
Hit-Iraq.evidence_basis: Bitumen-spring stronghold and river-ordeal center on the Middle Euphrates (~30-40 ha mounded river town attested continuously from Ebla/Mari texts through Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian itineraries; ~160 inh/ha).

Tell es-Sweyhat-Syria.name: Tell es-Sweyhat
Tell es-Sweyhat-Syria.evidence_basis: 45 ha rampart-enclosed Early Bronze Age steppe-margin town with excavated outer lower town and administrative buildings (Zettler 1997; Wilkinson 2004; Holland 2006; ~140 inh/ha), declining rapidly after 2000 BC.

Tell Barri-Syria.name: Tell Barri
Tell Barri-Syria.evidence_basis: 37 ha main tell plus 7 ha lower town on the Wadi Jaghjagh continuously occupied from EBA through Mitanni, Middle/Neo-Assyrian palace levels, and Neo-Babylonian eras (Pecorella and Pierobon Benoit 2005; ~145 inh/ha).

Eridu-Iraq.name: Eridu
Eridu-Iraq.evidence_basis: Earliest Enki sanctuary spanning ~40 ha in Late Ubaid-Late Uruk (Safar et al. 1981; Wright 1981; ~140 inh/ha), shrinking to a sacred ziggurat enclave of 8-22 ha after shifting Euphrates channels and marsh encroachment.

Hindanu-Iraq.name: Hindanu
Hindanu-Iraq.evidence_basis: Middle Euphrates caravan and provincial center at the desert-route junction (~30-40 ha tell complex attested in Mari texts and Neo-Assyrian tribute lists of Tukulti-Ninurta II and Ashurnasirpal II; ~155 inh/ha).

Tell al-Lahm-Iraq.name: Tell al-Lahm
Tell al-Lahm-Iraq.evidence_basis: 35-40 ha marsh-margin tell southeast of Ur guarding the southern Sealand waterways (Safar 1949; Hritz et al. 2012; ~145 inh/ha), flourishing during the First Sealand Dynasty and Neo-Babylonian eras.

Tell Gomel-Iraq.name: Tell Gomel
Tell Gomel-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~38-40 ha primary regional tell on the Khazir River surveyed by the Land of Nineveh Archaeological Project with sustained Bronze Age and Neo-Assyrian urban occupation (Morandi Bonacossi 2016; ~145 inh/ha).

Tell Mohammed Diyab-Syria.name: Tell Mohammed Diyab
Tell Mohammed Diyab-Syria.evidence_basis: ~35-40 ha Upper Khabur urban center southeast of Tell Leilan with excavated EBA, Old Babylonian Khabur Ware, and Mitanni neighborhoods (Nicolle 2006; ~145 inh/ha).

Ishchali-Iraq.name: Ishchali
Ishchali-Iraq.evidence_basis: 23 ha walled Diyala urban center housing the monumental Kititum Temple complex (Hill et al. 1990; Adams 1965; ~225 inh/ha at Old Babylonian height), declining after Eshnunna's fall.

Tell al-Rimah-Iraq.name: Tell al-Rimah
Tell al-Rimah-Iraq.evidence_basis: 25-28 ha circular walled city south of Jebel Sinjar featuring a monumental Old Babylonian palace, spiral-columned temple, and Neo-Assyrian stele (Oates 1968; Postgate et al. 1997; ~180 inh/ha).

Tikrit-Iraq.name: Tikrit
Tikrit-Iraq.evidence_basis: Cliff-top Tigris fortress-town (~25-30 ha fortified citadel and lower town) documented in the Babylonian Chronicle for Nabopolassar's 615 BC siege of the Assyrian garrison (~155 inh/ha).

Nuzi-Iraq.name: Nuzi
Nuzi-Iraq.evidence_basis: 4 ha fortified inner citadel plus ~16-20 ha of excavated Mitanni-period suburban estates and workshops (Starr 1939; Morrison 1993; ~200 inh/ha), documented by over 5,000 cuneiform tablets before Assyrian destruction c. 1340 BC.

Tell Arbid-Syria.name: Tell Arbid
Tell Arbid-Syria.evidence_basis: 38 ha tell complex (12 ha main mound + four lower mounds) with intensive Ninevite 5, EJ III-IV, Khabur Ware, and Mitanni occupation (Kolinski 2007; Bielinski 2010; ~135 inh/ha).

Tell Sifr-Iraq.name: Tell Sifr
Tell Sifr-Iraq.evidence_basis: Satellite town of Larsa covering ~25-30 ha, well documented by Old Babylonian private real-estate archives and copper hoards (Loftus; Charpin 1980; ~155 inh/ha), declining after Babylonian conquest.

Shibaniba-Iraq.name: Shibaniba
Shibaniba-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~18-22 ha multi-period Nineveh Plains provincial town excavated from Ninevite 5 through Middle and Neo-Assyrian administrative levels (Speiser 1933; Finkelstein 1953; ~190 inh/ha).

Grai Resh-Iraq.name: Grai Resh
Grai Resh-Iraq.evidence_basis: 32 ha Late Chalcolithic urban hub at the head of Wadi Tharthar with high mound tripartite feasting hall and obsidian workshops (Kepinski 2009, 2011; McMahon 2020; ~130 inh/ha), contracting in the early third millennium.

Tell Munbaqa-Syria.name: Tell Munbaqa
Tell Munbaqa-Syria.evidence_basis: 18-22 ha walled Euphrates city with extensively excavated Late Bronze Age domestic quarters and temples (Machule 1998; Werner 2004; ~185 inh/ha), abandoned during the c. 1200 BC collapse.

Tell Beydar-Syria.name: Tell Beydar
Tell Beydar-Syria.evidence_basis: 25-28 ha circular Kranzhugel provincial center of Nagar with excavated palace, temples, and EJ IIIb cuneiform archive (Lebeau and Suleiman 2003; Ur and Wilkinson 2008; ~145 inh/ha), abandoned c. 2200 BC with minor later villages.

Arzuhin-Iraq.name: Arzuhin
other_names: perhaps Gök tepe near Altun Kopru

Tell Hammam et-Turkman-Syria.name: Tell Hammam et-Turkman
Tell Hammam et-Turkman-Syria.evidence_basis: ~18-20 ha Balikh Valley center with LC2 niched monumental building and MBA palace (Van Loon 1988; Akkermans 1988; ~175 inh/ha), continuing through Mitanni/LBA.

Habuba Kabira-Syria.name: Habuba Kabira
Habuba Kabira-Syria.evidence_basis: 18-22 ha planned walled southern Uruk trade colony on the Syrian Euphrates with tripartite houses, temples, and drainage systems (Strommenger 1980; Vallet 1996; ~170 inh/ha), abruptly abandoned c. 3100 BC.

Tell Khaiber-Iraq.name: Tell Khaiber
Tell Khaiber-Iraq.evidence_basis: Excavated ~18 ha Sealand Dynasty administrative center 19 km northwest of Ur featuring a monumental fortified complex and cuneiform archive (Campbell et al. 2017; ~165 inh/ha).

Usiyeh-Iraq.name: Usiyeh
Usiyeh-Iraq.evidence_basis: Salvage-excavated Middle Euphrates terrace town of ~18-20 ha in the Haditha Basin with MBA monumental architecture, terracotta lions, and Middle/Neo-Assyrian fortifications (Fujii et al. 1985; ~155 inh/ha).

Chagar Bazar-Syria.name: Chagar Bazar
Chagar Bazar-Syria.evidence_basis: 12-15 ha Upper Khabur tell excavated with EBA and Shamshi-Adad I administrative archives (Mallowan 1947; Tunca et al. 2007; ~205 inh/ha at Old Babylonian peak).

Tell Agrab-Iraq.name: Tell Agrab
Tell Agrab-Iraq.evidence_basis: Rectangular walled Diyala town covering 10.8-14 ha dominated by the monumental Shara Temple (Delougaz and Lloyd 1942; Adams 1965; ~210 inh/ha in ED II-III), largely abandoned after Isin-Larsa.

Tell Kunara-Iraq.name: Tell Kunara
Tell Kunara-Iraq.evidence_basis: 10-12 ha monumental Early Bronze Age/Lullubi city in the Tanjaro Valley with stone-founded public buildings and cuneiform flour-ration tablets (Tenu 2019; ~200 inh/ha).

Tell Shemshara-Iraq.name: Tell Shemshara
Tell Shemshara-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~12 ha Rania Plain regional seat of Turukkean/Old Assyrian administration yielding the Shemshara royal palace archive (Ingholt 1957; Eidem and Laessoe 2001; ~195 inh/ha).

Kharaba Tibn or Tell Abu Hajar-Iraq.name: Kharaba Tibn or Tell Abu Hajar

Tell Uqair-Iraq.name: Tell Uqair
Tell Uqair-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~12-15 ha town north of Cutha noted for its Late Uruk Painted Temple and Jemdet Nasr-Old Babylonian occupation (Lloyd and Safar 1943; Adams 1972; ~160 inh/ha).

Tell Shelgiyya-Iraq.name: Tell Shelgiyya
Tell Shelgiyya-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~12-15 ha Upper Tigris Zammar-region mound excavated as an early Uruk Sprig Ware manufacturing hub with Ninevite 5 and Neo-Assyrian strata (Ball 1997, 2003; ~155 inh/ha).

Tell Yelkhi-Iraq.name: Tell Yelkhi
Tell Yelkhi-Iraq.evidence_basis: Excavated ~8-10 ha fortified Hamrin Basin town with Old Babylonian palace, temple, and Kassite administrative strata (Invernizzi 1980; Bergamini 1985; ~195 inh/ha).

Tell Mohammed Arab-Iraq.name: Tell Mohammed Arab
Tell Mohammed Arab-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~10 ha Eski Mosul Dam salvage-excavated Tigris settlement with dense Ninevite 5 and Middle Assyrian residential horizons (Roaf 1984; ~195 inh/ha).

Tell al-Daim-Iraq.name: Tell al-Daim
Tell al-Daim-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~10 ha excavated East-Tigris town and Neo-Assyrian fortified residence along the Little Zab-Arrapha road (al-Tekriti 1960; ~190 inh/ha).

Shaduppum-Iraq.name: Shaduppum
Shaduppum-Iraq.evidence_basis: Compact ~2 ha fortified administrative citadel plus surrounding Old Babylonian residential quarter (~8 ha total; Baqir 1946; Adams 1965; ~220 inh/ha), famous for the Laws of Eshnunna and mathematical tablets.

Tell Zeidan-Syria.name: Tell Zeidan
Tell Zeidan-Syria.evidence_basis: 12.5 ha Ubaid-Late Chalcolithic proto-urban mound at the Balikh-Euphrates junction with metallurgical and administrative evidence (Stein 2012; ~145 inh/ha), abandoned before the third millennium.

Jemdet Nasr-Iraq.name: Jemdet Nasr
Jemdet Nasr-Iraq.evidence_basis: 7.5 ha mound northeast of Kish featuring a large proto-cuneiform administrative complex (Matthews 1992; ~200 inh/ha in Jemdet Nasr peak), largely abandoned during Early Dynastic I.

Haradu-Iraq.name: Haradu
Haradu-Iraq.evidence_basis: Planned square walled Old Babylonian fortress-town (~1.5 ha dense orthogonal grid plus riverfront suburbs totaling ~8-10 ha; Kepinski-Lecomte 1992; ~175 inh/ha), later reoccupied as a Middle Assyrian outpost.

Gurga Chiya-Iraq.name: Gurga Chiya
Gurga Chiya-Iraq.evidence_basis: ~5-6 ha multi-period Shahrizor Plain tell excavated with Late Uruk, Kassite/LBA, and Iron Age occupation strata (Wengrow et al. 2016; ~170 inh/ha).

Jebel Aruda-Syria.name: Jebel Aruda
Jebel Aruda-Syria.evidence_basis: 6-8 ha hilltop Late Uruk colonial administrative and temple complex overlooking the Euphrates (van Driel 2002; Vallet 1998; ~155 inh/ha), abandoned at the end of the Uruk Expansion c. 3100 BC.

Tell Sabi Abyad-Syria.name: Tell Sabi Abyad
Tell Sabi Abyad-Syria.evidence_basis: Excavated ~5 ha Middle Assyrian fortified dunnu estate and administrative center of the grand vizier Ili-pada with 400+ tablets (Akkermans and Wiggermann 2015; ~200 inh/ha including dependent workers).

Tell Mashnaqa-Syria.name: Tell Mashnaqa
Tell Mashnaqa-Syria.evidence_basis: Excavated 4 ha Middle Khabur settlement with LC3 terraced official building, large ovens, and Ninevite 5 storage installations (Beyer 1998; Thuesen 2000; McMahon 2020; ~170 inh/ha).
